questions.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions of the equation $4\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2\sqrt{5}=0$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘},$ what is the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, isolating $\operatorname{cos}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2\sqrt{5} & =0 \\ 4\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =2\sqrt{5} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{2})={60}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${60}^{∘}$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={60}^{∘}.$

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={60}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the fourth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={60}^{∘}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13952163/assets/9c8adbb0a1594ae5bacfab7f1f92993c67659839599e10ab46d5cf98896e3ec7.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $4$th quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={360}^{∘}-{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={360}^{∘}-{60}^{∘} \\  & ={300}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x={60}^{∘},\,{300}^{∘}.$

Finally, the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ is $60\cdot 300=18\,000.$

$$

$$

$$

questions.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{cos}⁡x=\frac{9}{11}$ for $0\le x<2\pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2},$ rounded to one decimal place?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{9}{11})=0.612\,554…≈0.612\,6\end{aligned}
$$

Since $0.612\,6$ lies inside the specified domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=0.612\,6.$

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=0.612\,6.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x>0,$ the second solution must lie in the fourth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=0.612\,6.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13952163/assets/23712114dae7013de5786e51b99cbd0857c41ed6443e0cb6a9f54aa4ba00dcbb.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$ lies in the $4$th quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -0.612\,6 \\  & ≈5.670\,6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=0.612\,6\cdot 5.670\,6≈3.5
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, isolating $\operatorname{cos}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+1 & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =-\frac{1}{4} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-\frac{1}{2})={120}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${120}^{∘}$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={120}^{∘}.$

Our first solution lies in the second quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={60}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={60}^{∘}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13952163/assets/ec1135cb0a4d35130a1c11baf9f421a3cdb4bc22cc1b436686dce722fa3c812e.png)

A second solution $X$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, and we can find it using the reference angle, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}X & ={180}^{∘}+{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={180}^{∘}+{60}^{∘} \\  & ={240}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

However, this value is not in the required domain. To get a second solution that's within the required domain, we simply subtract ${360}^{∘}$ from $X:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =X-{360}^{∘} \\  & ={240}^{∘}-{360}^{∘} \\  & =-{120}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=\pm {120}^{∘}.$

Finally, the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ is

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=120\cdot (-120)=-14\,400.
$$

First, we rearrange the equation, isolating $\operatorname{cos}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3 & =0 \\ 2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =-3 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x & =-\frac{3}{2\sqrt{3}} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})=\frac{5\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\frac{5\pi }{6}$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=\frac{5\pi }{6}.$

Our first solution lies in the second quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13952163/assets/6bc5aed39e6421b8ff2416edb75dc888c8f38ae14f99b3d6e28d8e4c9302908f.png)

A second solution $X$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, and we can find it using the reference angle, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

However, this value is not in the required domain. To get a second solution that's within the required domain, we simply subtract $2\pi $ from $X:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =X-2\pi  \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}-2\pi  \\  & =-\frac{5\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=\pm \frac{5\pi }{6}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}{x}_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6}\cdot (-\frac{5\pi }{6})=-\frac{25{\pi }^{2}}{36}.
$$

A second solution $X$ lies in the $4$th quadrant, and we can find it using the reference angle, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}X & ={360}^{∘}-{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={360}^{∘}-{45}^{∘} \\  & ={315}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

However, this value is not in the required domain. To get a second solution that's within the required domain, we simply subtract ${360}^{∘}$ from $X:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =X-{360}^{∘} \\  & ={315}^{∘}-{360}^{∘} \\  & =-{45}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=\pm {45}^{∘}.$

Finally, the numerical value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$ is

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=45\cdot (-45)=-2\,025.
$$

questions.problem:
Arranged in **ascending order**, the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0$ for $-\pi \le x<\pi $ are $x=${{field-1}} and $x=$
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the solutions to $\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0$ correspond to the roots of $\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ 

First, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(0)=\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\frac{\pi }{2}$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

This solution is a quadrantal angle. To find all solutions, we use our knowledge of the cosine function. We know that the cosine function has its roots at

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi .
$$

Therefore, to find the second solution ${x}_{2}$ in the given range, we set $n=-1$ and we get

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{2}-\pi =-\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, the solutions of the equation, arranged in ascending order, are $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =2 \\ -2\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the solutions to $\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0$ correspond to the roots of $\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ 

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(0)={90}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${90}^{∘}$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}={90}^{∘}.$

This solution is a quadrantal angle. To find the remaining solutions, we use our knowledge of the cosine function. We know that the cosine function has its roots at

$$
x={90}^{∘}+{180}^{∘}\cdot n.
$$

Therefore, to find the other solution ${x}_{2}$ in the given range, we set $n=1,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={90}^{∘}+{180}^{∘}={270}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x={90}^{∘},\,{270}^{∘}.$

$$

This solution is a quadrantal angle. To find the remaining solutions, we use our knowledge of the cosine function. We know that the cosine function has its maximum values at

$$
x={360}^{∘}\cdot n.
$$

Since the domain $-{180}^{∘}<x\le {180}^{∘}$ is one period, and we have already found one maximum value in this period, we conclude that $x={0}^{∘}$ is the only solution.

canonical_examples.problem: Find the solutions to the equation $2\cos{x}+\sqrt{2}=0$ for $0 \leq x <      2\pi.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, isolating $\cos x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\sqrt{2} & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =-\sqrt{2} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})=\frac{3\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ lies inside the specified domain, our first solution is $x_1 = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}.$

Our first solution lies in the second quadrant and has a reference angle of $\theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$ Since $\cos{x} < 0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle $\theta_R = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13952163/assets/bf1efb64724fb0dfbf60cc14905e63ba867caa0bf0edd888b35fb554af97c856.png)

Since the second solution $x_2$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{5\pi}{4}.$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{4}{5})=0.643\,501…≈0.644\end{aligned}
$$

Since $0.644$ lies inside the given domain, our first solution is $x_1 = 0.644.$

Our first solution lies in the first quadrant and has a reference angle of $\theta_R = 0.644.$ Since $\cos{x} > 0,$ the second solution must lie in the fourth quadrant, and it also has a reference angle $\theta_R = 0.644.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13952163/assets/8ec2e836cb0db78f0811bf8256ec1ab08323b9f3adfe9bd127a8911ece7ee3bd.png)

Since the second solution $x_2$ lies in the $4$th quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -0.644 \\  & =5.639\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions (rounded to one decimal place) are $x = 0.6, 5.6.$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Since $135^\circ$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is $x_1 = 135^\circ.$

Our first solution lies in the second quadrant and has a reference angle of $\theta_R = 45^\circ.$ Since $\cos{x} <    0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle $\theta_R = 45^\circ.$

A second solution $X$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, and we can find it using the reference angle, as follows:

$$

$$

However, this value is not in the required domain. To get a second solution that's within the required domain, we subtract $360^\circ$ from $X \mathbin{:}$

$$

$$

So, the solutions are $x = - 135^\circ , 135^\circ.$
